network.overall_strategy: Construct ten explicitly distinguished route variants, not ten independently demonstrated prebiotic mechanisms. Four variants represent experimentally observed discharge syntheses using different gas mixtures. Two begin with acetone photohomologation and diverge into aminonitrile hydrolysis or a less-supported hydantoin route. Four use alternative reductive-amination systems downstream of a hypothetical isovalerate-to-alpha-ketoisocaproate transformation. Ni, meteoritic Fe-Ni and Pd variants are distinct catalytic implementations of the same amination chemistry. The isovalerate carboxylation remains an unresolved carbon-skeleton bottleneck, so those four pathways are conditional, not demonstrated end-to-end syntheses. Starting inventories include small gases, acetone, isobutane and externally supplied isovaleric acid; their availability is not equivalent to selective synthesis from C1 feedstocks. Discharge reactions and photoreductive homologations are explicitly coarse-grained transformations. Their listed small coproducts provide formal atom/redox bookkeeping, not measured product distributions. All routes are anoxic and predict racemic leucine without an additional symmetry-breaking process. Neutral molecular formulas represent aqueous acid-base pools. The schema lacks a byproduct role, so coproduct-only species are labelled intermediate. A null environment_formed denotes an external inventory or formation in multiple environments. The network exceeds the suggested minimum size to represent the ten variants and their limitations explicitly.

molecules.common_name: elemental sulfur; formal zero-valent sulfur sink

reactions.name: Methane-nitrogen discharge synthesis with aqueous processing

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K aqueous collection; nonthermal electrical discharge
conditions.other: Anoxic CH4/N2 atmosphere with trace NH3 and an aqueous trap. Endpoint includes aqueous reactions and hydrolytic workup. The stated collection range is an environmental analogue, not a reconstruction of every experimental workup temperature.

reactions.mechanism: Coarse-grained empirical process: discharge generates a complex carbon-nitrogen inventory, followed by aqueous amino-acid-precursor chemistry and hydrolysis. A Strecker contribution is plausible, but the leucine-specific carbon-skeleton sequence was not resolved.
reactions.reasoning: Leucine was detected in methane-based discharge experiments (Ring et al., 1972; Ring and Miller, 1984). Methane runs produced approximately 1.4-7.6 leucine molecules per 100 glycine molecules, with poor constitutional-isomer selectivity. This node represents the observed overall process, not a demonstrated elementary conversion. H2 and CO2 are formal small-product bookkeeping species, not a complete measured discharge product distribution. Locally reducing atmospheres are required.

reactions.name: Isobutane-fed discharge synthesis with aqueous processing

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K aqueous collection; nonthermal electrical discharge
conditions.other: Anoxic hydrocarbon/nitrogen discharge with an ammonia-containing aqueous trap and subsequent hydrolysis. A pre-existing isobutane inventory is assumed, not generated by this network.

reactions.mechanism: Electrical fragmentation and recombination of a branched hydrocarbon feed produce an unresolved mixture of carbonyl and nitrogenous precursors, some of which yield leucine during aqueous processing.
reactions.reasoning: Ring and Miller (1984) reported leucine at approximately 6.7 per 100 glycine for an isobutane feed. This supports a distinct feedstock-dependent process variant, but not selective preservation of the isobutane branch or a resolved mechanism. The geological abundance of the starting hydrocarbon remains a constraint. Listed coproducts are formal bookkeeping rather than a measured closed product inventory.

reactions.name: Acetylene-fed discharge synthesis with aqueous processing

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K aqueous collection; nonthermal electrical discharge
conditions.other: Anoxic acetylene-containing discharge and aqueous precursor collection, followed by hydrolysis. An external acetylene supply is required.

reactions.mechanism: Discharge-driven reactions of unsaturated C2 fragments generate larger carbon skeletons and nitrogenous precursors; subsequent aqueous processing releases a minor leucine fraction.
reactions.reasoning: Ring and Miller (1984) reported approximately 14 leucine molecules per 100 glycine molecules in an acetylene experiment. This is stronger relative production than in the cited methane runs, but does not establish absolute efficiency or branched-skeleton selectivity. The reaction remains an empirical process-level node; H2 and CO2 represent formal small-product bookkeeping.

reactions.name: Hydrogen-sulfide-rich volcanic discharge synthesis

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K aqueous collection; reference apparatus included water boiling near 373 K
conditions.other: Locally reducing CH4/H2S/NH3/CO2 gas mixture, electrical discharge and an aqueous trap. The historical experiment operated for three days. H2S is a reactive feedstock, not a catalyst.

reactions.mechanism: Coarse-grained discharge and aqueous synthesis. Sulfur-derived radicals may facilitate alkyl-radical chemistry and formation of branched carbonyl precursors, followed by amino-acid-precursor formation and hydrolysis.
reactions.reasoning: Leucine was identified in the reanalysis of Miller's 1958 H2S-rich experiment (Parker et al., 2011, PNAS). Sulfur-assisted alkyl-radical formation is a mechanistic proposal rather than a resolved leucine pathway (Parker et al., 2011, Origins of Life and Evolution of Biospheres). The mixture need not represent the global atmosphere. S8 is a formal zero-valent sulfur endpoint; actual sulfur speciation and the full discharge product inventory are not asserted.

reactions.name: Acetone cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: Concentrated aqueous acetone and HCN/CN- pool; approximately neutral to mildly alkaline pH. The subsequent reduction is needed to draw the reversible addition forward.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the acetone carbonyl, followed by proton transfer to form the cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: Acetone cyanohydrin formation initiates the branched amino-acid branch in Patel et al. (2015). Its equilibrium abundance can be limited, and downstream consumption helps pull the addition forward. Acetone is deliberately treated as a supplied C3 feedstock rather than claiming that this graph establishes its selective synthesis from C1 compounds.

reactions.name: First deoxygenative photoreduction to the C4 aldehyde

conditions.other: Anoxic, UV-illuminated sulfide-containing water; laboratory evidence uses 254 nm irradiation. Staged sulfur addition and photoreduction are represented as one net transformation.

reactions.mechanism: Coarse-grained sulfur-assisted deoxygenation and nitrile-derived reduction/hydrolysis produce the C4 aldehyde equivalent. Short-lived sulfur-containing intermediates are not represented as separately quantified products.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015), reviewed by Green et al. (2021), support the staged chemistry leading from acetone cyanohydrin to the next aldehyde-derived cyanohydrin. Separating the transient aldehyde into its own node enables carbon mapping; it does not claim selective isolation of that aldehyde. S8 represents a formal S(0) redox sink, not verified sulfur-product speciation. Sulfide availability and copper sequestration constrain geological operation (Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Cyanide trapping of isobutyraldehyde

conditions.other: HCN/CN- available to trap the transient aldehyde; approximately neutral to mildly alkaline solution.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanide addition to 2-methylpropanal generates 2-hydroxy-3-methylbutanenitrile.
reactions.reasoning: The isobutyraldehyde cyanohydrin is an experimentally supported branch point in Patel et al. (2015). Here it is retained for a further homologation instead of diverting it toward the valine aminonitrile. This chemical choice is required to extend the skeleton toward leucine.

reactions.name: Second deoxygenative photoreduction to the C5 aldehyde

conditions.other: Staged sulfide chemistry and UV exposure; laboratory precedent uses 254 nm irradiation. Conditions must avoid uncontrolled diversion into other sulfur or cyanide products.

reactions.mechanism: Net transformation through sulfur-containing intermediates removes the alpha hydroxyl functionality and converts the nitrile-derived carbon into an aldehyde, yielding the 3-methylbutanal equivalent.
reactions.reasoning: The additional sulfur-mediated photochemical cycle leading toward the leucine aminonitrile is supported by Patel et al. (2015) and Green et al. (2021). The C5 aldehyde is represented as the carbonyl equivalent subsequently trapped by cyanide, not as a reported high-yield isolated feedstock. This is a central skeleton-building bottleneck: staged handling, realistic UV rates and full-sequence leucine-specific yield remain unresolved. S8 is formal sulfur bookkeeping.

reactions.name: Formation of the leucine-skeleton cyanohydrin

conditions.other: Aqueous HCN/CN- trapping of the C5 aldehyde; no chiral directing agent.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to 3-methylbutanal to furnish racemic 2-hydroxy-4-methylpentanenitrile.
reactions.reasoning: The cyanohydrin immediately preceding leucine aminonitrile formation is described in Patel et al. (2015). This reaction establishes the C6 skeleton, but continued hydrolysis without sufficient ammonia would favor the corresponding alpha-hydroxy acid rather than leucine.

reactions.name: Ammonia-mediated formation of leucine alpha-aminonitrile

conditions.other: Ammonia-rich stage following photochemistry; pH and total ammonia must provide an appreciable free-NH3 concentration. Protect accumulated aminonitrile from unnecessary further irradiation.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanohydrin dissociation, carbonyl-imine chemistry and cyanide capture give the alpha-aminonitrile. The net transformation is not assumed to be direct substitution of an unactivated hydroxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) report the leucine alpha-aminonitrile precursor after ammonia addition. This is stronger evidence than an assertion of leucine itself as the photochemical endpoint. Ammonia availability controls competition with cyanohydrin persistence and hydroxy-acid formation.

reactions.name: Hydration of leucine aminonitrile to leucinamide
agents: Hydronium ions supplied by an acidic aqueous setting

conditions.other: Proposed acidic volcanic-water stage, approximately pH 1-3; prolonged residence may be necessary. These are candidate natural conditions, not a reported leucine-specific kinetic measurement.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-assisted nitrile hydration produces the primary carboxamide through imidate-like intermediates.
reactions.reasoning: Nitrile-to-amide hydrolysis is the chemically expected first stage of Strecker-product hydrolysis (Miller, 1957). However, the supplied Patel et al. (2015) evidence ends at the aminonitrile. Conversion rates and yields for this particular intermediate under the stated natural conditions are therefore an extrapolation, not a demonstrated continuation of the photochemical sequence.

reactions.name: Leucinamide hydrolysis to racemic leucine
agents: Hydronium ions supplied by an acidic aqueous setting

conditions.other: Continue aqueous hydrolysis, then cool or dilute. Ammonia is represented in neutral form although ammonium predominates in the acidic solution.

reactions.mechanism: Water attacks the protonated amide carbonyl, followed by C-N cleavage to give leucine and ammonium/ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: This is the conventional completion of aminonitrile hydrolysis in Strecker chemistry (Miller, 1957). It is chemically well founded but is not a reported leucine-specific endpoint of Patel et al. (2015). The full photochemical-plus-hydrolysis yield is unknown, and unnecessarily prolonged heating risks product degradation (Aubrey et al., 2009).

reactions.name: Alternative Bucherer-Bergs capture of isovaleraldehyde

conditions.other: Concentrated aldehyde, cyanide and ammonia/carbonate inventory. Carbonate is a reagent reservoir, not a mineral catalyst. Substrate-specific conditions remain to be established.

reactions.mechanism: Aminonitrile formation, incorporation of a CO2-derived carbamoyl carbon and cyclization give 5-isobutylhydantoin. This node groups the standard multistep reaction class.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative leucine-specific extension, included because an aldehyde-derived hydantoin is a chemically credible alternative reservoir for the same amino-acid skeleton. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) provide related cyanide/ammonia/hydantoin chemistry for alpha-keto acids, but that work does not establish this aldehyde substrate or this leucine route. Hydantoin trapping could improve precursor persistence while making final hydrolysis more difficult.

reactions.name: Hydantoin ring opening and decarbamoylation to leucine

conditions.other: Proposed alkaline aqueous processing with possible subsequent pH change for decarbamoylation. This is not a validated single-condition protocol. Rapid cooling after product formation would limit thermal loss.

reactions.mechanism: Coarse-grained hydantoin ring hydrolysis through an N-carbamoyl amino-acid intermediate, followed by removal of the carbamoyl group, releases leucine, ammonia and inorganic carbon.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative under the stated prebiotic conditions: the supplied research does not demonstrate hydrolysis of 5-isobutylhydantoin. The hydantoin chemistry of Pulletikurti et al. (2022) cannot be assumed to give the same rate for this structurally different substrate. Ring opening and especially complete deprotection may require harsher conditions than are geochemically useful; competing leucine degradation is a major limitation (Aubrey et al., 2009).

reactions.name: Hypothetical pyrite-coupled reductive carboxylation of isovalerate
agents: Iron monosulfide consumed during proposed pyrite-forming redox coupling

conditions.other: Anoxic FeS/H2S/CO2-containing water with a supplied isovalerate inventory. No validated catalyst, activation sequence, rate or yield exists for this transformation. The stated conditions are hypotheses, not experimental findings.

reactions.mechanism: Formal net coupling of reductive C1 insertion at the isovalerate carboxyl group to FeS/H2S conversion into pyrite. A chemically effective acyl-activation and C-C-bond-forming mechanism remains unidentified.
reactions.reasoning: Explicitly speculative. Keefe, Lazcano and Miller (1995) proposed reductive carboxylation of branched fatty acids and discussed pyrite formation as a possible source of reducing power, while stating that prebiotic conditions remained to be worked out. Isovalerate occurs in meteoritic inventories, but its presence does not demonstrate this reaction. Stoichiometric balance and possible redox driving force do not establish kinetics. Every pathway using this node is conditional on solving this bottleneck.

reactions.name: Nickel-catalysed hydrogenative amination of alpha-ketoisocaproate

conditions.other: Approximately pH 8; reported benchmark uses 0.03 M keto acid, five equivalents of NH4HCO3, approximately 10 mol% Ni and 72 hours. This is a cool, pressurized aqueous-interface analogue, not hot-vent chemistry.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia reacts with the alpha-keto group to form an imine/iminium pool, followed by surface-mediated H2 activation and reduction to leucine.
reactions.reasoning: Leucine formation from alpha-ketoisocaproate was demonstrated by Kaur et al. (2024), with no reaction in metal-free controls. Nickel is justified by this substrate-specific evidence. The supported laboratory catalyst is not automatically equivalent to a natural mineral. Competing hydroxy-acid formation is represented separately, and the reported multi-substrate yield range must not be assigned as a leucine-specific yield. This validates amination, not rxn_015.

reactions.name: Meteoritic Fe-Ni-catalysed hydrogenative amination
agents: Ground Aletai iron meteorite containing metallic Fe-Ni phases

conditions.other: Approximately pH 8; 0.03 M keto acid, five equivalents of NH4HCO3 and 72 hours in the reported benchmark. Catalyst loading was expressed as approximately 18 mol% Ni.

reactions.mechanism: Heterogeneous activation of H2 on meteoritic metallic phases supplies reducing equivalents for the ammonia-derived imine intermediate.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated amino-acid synthesis, including leucine, using ground iron-meteorite material. This is a separate experimentally tested catalytic implementation, not a separate carbon-skeleton mechanism. Meteoritic Fe-Ni has a more direct natural analogue than an engineered support, although reactive surface area, passivation and reactant concentration remain important. Amino- and hydroxy-acid competition remains substantial.

reactions.name: Palladium-catalysed hydrogenative amination benchmark

conditions.other: Approximately pH 8; 0.03 M keto acid, five equivalents of NH4HCO3, approximately 1 mol% Pd and 72 hours in the reported benchmark.

reactions.mechanism: Pd activates H2 and reduces the ammonia-derived imine pool, favoring amino-acid formation over direct carbonyl reduction under the reported conditions.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated this substrate-to-leucine conversion. Across the tested substrates, Pd gave higher amino-acid selectivity than Ni or meteorite catalysts, but those aggregate values are not leucine-specific yields. Pd/C is retained as a chemically informative experimental alternative, not assigned equal geological likelihood: palladium is scarce and the engineered catalyst requires a natural analogue. The upstream skeleton bottleneck is unchanged.

reactions.name: Proposed pyrite-coupled reductive amination of alpha-ketoisocaproate
agents: Fresh iron monosulfide as a redox-active, consumed mineral agent

conditions.other: Anoxic FeS/H2S mixture, alkaline ammonia-containing solution, approximately pH 9-10. Earlier related systems used much higher ammonia concentrations than the mild H2/metal experiments. FeS is represented as a reactant because it is consumed.

reactions.mechanism: Formal coupling of imine reduction to pyrite formation from FeS and H2S supplies the reducing equivalents otherwise supplied by molecular hydrogen.
reactions.reasoning: Hafenbradl et al. (1995) described pyrite-associated reductive amination, and Huber and Wachtershauser (2003) demonstrated related alpha-keto-acid aminations with freshly precipitated iron phases. The provided evidence does not establish this exact alpha-ketoisocaproate/FeS/H2S combination, so the leucine-specific transformation and conditions are speculative extensions. High ammonia demand, mineral passivation and thermal decomposition may prevent useful accumulation.

reactions.name: Competing nickel-catalysed reduction to alpha-hydroxyisocaproate

conditions.other: Competes with rxn_016 in the ammonia-containing reaction mixture. The hydroxy acid is treated as a competing sink, not automatically recycled to keto acid.

reactions.mechanism: Direct hydrogenation of the alpha-keto carbonyl produces the alpha-hydroxy acid instead of reducing an ammonia-derived imine.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) observed competing hydroxy-acid formation during hydrogenative amination. Ni and meteorite experiments gave approximately comparable amino- and hydroxy-acid production across the studied substrate set, but an exact leucine-specific branching ratio is not available in the supplied evidence. Including this chemically required competitor prevents interpreting all keto-acid consumption as leucine production.

pathways.name: Methane-discharge process
pathways.description: Observed overall production from a methane/nitrogen/ammonia/water inventory. The single graph reaction is an explicitly coarse-grained discharge, aqueous-processing and hydrolysis sequence; the leucine-specific intermediates were not resolved.

pathways.name: Isobutane-discharge process
pathways.description: Observed feedstock-dependent discharge variant using a supplied branched C4 hydrocarbon. It differs from P1 in carbon inventory, not in a demonstrated unique terminal amino-acid mechanism.

pathways.name: Acetylene-discharge process
pathways.description: Observed discharge variant using an unsaturated C2 feedstock. Leucine is a minor component of a complex product inventory, and the branched-skeleton assembly sequence remains unresolved.

pathways.name: Sulfide-rich volcanic discharge process
pathways.description: Observed leucine production in the archived H2S-rich discharge experiment. Sulfur-assisted alkyl-radical chemistry is a proposed explanation, not a fully established molecular route.

pathways.name: Acetone photohomologation followed by aminonitrile hydrolysis
pathways.description: Build the branched skeleton through two sulfur-assisted photochemical cycles, trap the C5 aldehyde with cyanide, form the demonstrated leucine aminonitrile, and hydrolyse it through leucinamide. The aminonitrile endpoint is supported; the complete natural-condition sequence to leucine and its overall yield are not demonstrated. Transfer to acidic water is required by the proposed hydrolysis stage.

pathways.name: Acetone photohomologation followed by hydantoin chemistry
pathways.description: Share the chemically required C5 aldehyde-building sequence with P5, then divert the aldehyde into a hydantoin rather than the isolated aminonitrile branch. The leucine-specific hydantoin formation and hydrolysis are speculative under prebiotic conditions. Warmer aqueous processing is proposed because hydantoin deprotection is a separate kinetic bottleneck.

pathways.name: Conditional isovalerate carboxylation plus supported-Ni amination
pathways.description: Begin with an externally supplied isovalerate inventory. Hypothetical pyrite-coupled carboxylation supplies alpha-ketoisocaproate, which must be cooled or transferred to the mild H2/Ni reaction setting. The final amination is experimentally supported; the upstream carbon-skeleton transformation is not.

pathways.name: Conditional isovalerate carboxylation plus meteoritic Fe-Ni amination
pathways.description: Use the same unresolved carboxylation as P7, followed by the independently tested ground-meteorite catalytic implementation of hydrogenative amination. Cooling, H2 supply and a reactive metallic surface are necessary. This is a catalyst-resolved variant, not an independently established skeleton-building pathway.

pathways.name: Conditional isovalerate carboxylation plus Pd amination
pathways.description: Combine the hypothetical keto-acid supply with experimentally supported Pd/C hydrogenative amination. This is an experimentally informative, potentially more selective catalyst variant, but Pd scarcity and the absence of a demonstrated natural catalyst analogue lower its geochemical priority.

pathways.name: Conditional pyrite-coupled skeleton formation and amination
pathways.description: Form the keto acid by the unresolved isovalerate carboxylation hypothesis, then test FeS/H2S-driven reductive amination without requiring externally supplied H2 for the amination step. Both the upstream skeleton transformation and the exact leucine-specific mineral amination require experimental validation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Methane-discharge production of leucine is supported by Ring et al. (1972) and Ring & Miller (1984). However, the supplied authoritative balance check identifies rxn_001 as UNBALANCED, making P1 invalid as encoded. This low score concerns the submitted reaction representation, not the experimental existence of methane-discharge leucine synthesis. Surface discharge and aqueous processing are plausible, but the operating and hydrolysis conditions are unspecified.
suggestions: Correct rxn_001 and rerun the balance check. Investigate the checker's hinted NH3-product and CO2/CO-reactant alternatives, but do not treat those hints as experimentally justified corrections.
Provide explicit stoichiometric bookkeeping, gas partial pressures, aqueous-trap conditions and the post-discharge hydrolysis protocol.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ring & Miller (1984) support leucine production with an isobutane feed. The supplied check confirms that rxn_002 is balanceable, and its explicitly aggregate interpretation is appropriate. Neither externally supplied isobutane nor low product selectivity invalidates this route. Remaining limitations are the missing experimental conditions and the distinction between discharge products and leucine recovered after aqueous workup.
suggestions: Record the checker-provided coefficients and attach the isobutane-specific experimental citation.
Specify discharge duration, gas composition, trap pH and hydrolysis conditions, distinguishing laboratory workup from an environmentally justified implementation.
Report leucine recovery and isomer distribution without interpreting the bookkeeping equation as a measured product distribution.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The acetylene-fed discharge variant has direct leucine evidence in Ring & Miller (1984), and rxn_003 passes the supplied balanceability test. It is defensible as an aggregate experimental process rather than an elementary reaction. Its environmental implementation remains incompletely specified, especially the aqueous processing needed to recover the amino acid.
suggestions: Add the inferred coefficients and the acetylene-specific experimental conditions.
Define gas retention, discharge exposure, aqueous composition and hydrolysis conditions.
Distinguish glycine-normalized leucine abundance from absolute yield or conversion of acetylene.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Parker et al. (2011, PNAS) directly support leucine formation in the H2S-rich discharge experiment. rxn_004 is balanceable according to the supplied check, and the network appropriately identifies its sulfur and hydrogen coproducts as formal bookkeeping. A locally reducing discharge setting is plausible, but the broad Surface label does not establish the experimental gas mixture, energy input or processing conditions. This is the strongest documented complete-process variant in the submitted network.
suggestions: Specify gas partial pressures, discharge duration, boiling-water and collection conditions, and any post-discharge hydrolysis.
Describe how locally reducing gases and sulfide are maintained without assuming a globally reducing atmosphere.
Keep S8 and H2 coefficients explicitly separate from claims about measured sulfur speciation or product yields.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The carbon-skeleton progression and aminonitrile identity are coherent with Patel et al. (2015) and Green, Xu & Sutherland (2021). The photoreductions are acceptable as explicitly coarse-grained transformations, not elementary mechanisms. However, the cited experimental endpoint is the leucine aminonitrile, not an integrated acetone-to-leucine preparation. Hydrolysis through leucinamide is chemically plausible, but its kinetics, conditions and compatibility with the preceding photochemical stages are not specified.
suggestions: Specify UV exposure, sulfide speciation, pH, sequential reagent additions and the tested Cu-assisted formulation, or justify a copper-free implementation.
Provide the conditions and reaction times for aminonitrile hydration and leucinamide hydrolysis rather than assuming rapid conversion in unspecified surface water.
Measure full-sequence leucine recovery and intermediate losses, while retaining the distinction between demonstrated precursor synthesis and proposed downstream processing.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Classical Bucherer-Bergs chemistry makes formation of the correctly identified 5-isobutylhydantoin plausible. The weaker link is its conversion to leucine under unspecified hydrothermal conditions. Evidence summarized for alpha-keto-acid-derived hydantoin chemistry in Pulletikurti et al. (2022) does not by itself establish the hydrolysis conditions for this aldehyde-derived hydantoin. Surface-to-hydrothermal transport, residence time and product survival are also unaddressed.
suggestions: Provide substrate-specific support and ammonium, carbonate, cyanide, pH and temperature conditions for rxn_013.
Demonstrate 5-isobutylhydantoin hydrolysis at the proposed temperature and pH, and record the two-water coefficient required for rxn_014.
Define the transport mechanism, dilution, residence time and competing degradation during hydrothermal processing.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) support nickel-catalysed conversion of supplied alpha-ketoisocaproate to leucine and the competing hydroxyacid branch. rxn_020 is scored here as a competing outcome, not a leucine-producing step. The complete pathway nevertheless depends on rxn_015, which is balanced but experimentally unresolved and lacks an established activation and C-C bond-forming mechanism for free isovalerate. Calling that step hypothetical is accurate but does not establish an executable route.
suggestions: Retain rxn_015 as a conditional hypothesis until selective alpha-ketoisocaproate formation and the required activation chemistry are demonstrated.
Specify a supported nickel formulation and an operating protocol comparable to the cited 22 °C, pH 8, 5 bar H2 experiments, including ammonium loading and reaction time.
Justify cooling and transfer from the sulfide-rich stage, test catalyst passivation by carried-over sulfur species, and quantify leucine versus hydroxyacid formation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ground iron meteorite catalysis of the terminal amination has experimental support in Kaur et al. (2024). That evidence does not supply the missing alpha-ketoisocaproate-producing chemistry in rxn_015. The meteorite designation also does not specify accessible metallic surface, weathering state or activity after contact with hydrothermal sulfide. This is a supported amination implementation attached to an unresolved upstream transformation.
suggestions: Specify Fe-Ni composition, accessible surface area, particle preparation and catalyst stability under the proposed aqueous conditions.
Resolve rxn_015 independently and define the cooling, transport, hydrogen-pressure and ammonium conditions for rxn_017.
Report catalyst-specific aminoacid versus hydroxyacid selectivity rather than assuming the nickel-only rxn_020 quantitatively represents meteorite catalysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Pd-catalysed amination is a legitimate, experimentally supported benchmark, with favorable aminoacid selectivity across the substrates studied by Kaur et al. (2024). Its strong downstream chemistry does not overcome the unresolved rxn_015. A laboratory benchmark is not automatically a natural catalytic setting: the catalyst formulation, availability and resistance to sulfur carryover remain unspecified. The low pathway score is driven primarily by the missing skeleton-forming reaction, not by choosing palladium.
suggestions: Keep the Pd branch explicitly identified as a benchmark unless a physically justified environmental catalyst inventory is supplied.
Provide the supported-catalyst formulation, hydrogen pressure, ammonium concentration, pH and reaction time, and assess sulfur poisoning during transfer.
Do not present the complete route as demonstrated until rxn_015 is experimentally established; distinguish leucine-specific yields from the published multi-substrate yield ranges.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Both reactions conserve atoms under the supplied check, and FeS and H2S are explicitly present. Nevertheless, pyrite formation does not establish kinetic coupling to selective isovalerate carboxylation. General FeS-mediated alpha-keto-acid amination evidence, including Huber & Wächtershäuser (2003), supports investigating rxn_019 but does not demonstrate this exact leucine-specific FeS/H2S-to-pyrite transformation. Hydrothermal temperature, pH and product-survival constraints are undefined.
suggestions: Demonstrate alpha-ketoisocaproate formation from the supplied isovalerate inventory, identifying activation chemistry and competing products.
Test rxn_019 separately with alpha-ketoisocaproate and establish reductant consumption, mineral transformation and leucine yield.
Specify temperature, pressure, pH, ammonia loading and residence time, and compare synthesis rates with precursor and leucine degradation.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network has sufficient size, consistent molecule identifiers and one connected molecule-reaction graph; terminal coproducts and the hydroxyacid branch are not isolated subgraphs. According to the authoritative check, 13 reactions are balanced as written, six are balanceable with coefficients, and rxn_001 is a conservation violation requiring correction. The larger coefficients associated with the formal S8 sink are not independently evidence of implausible chemistry. Literature alignment is substantial: the network correctly distinguishes observed discharge processes, demonstrated aminonitrile chemistry, supported terminal aminations and the unresolved isovalerate-to-ketoacid hypothesis. It also appropriately acknowledges racemic products and competing nickel reduction. However, reaction-level citations and operating protocols are absent, P5 extends beyond its cited experimental endpoint, P6 lacks substrate-specific hydrolysis validation, and P7-P10 all depend on the same unsupported rxn_015. That shared bottleneck is not four independent demonstrations or four independent failures. Environmental confidence is limited by missing temperature, pressure, pH, catalyst, irradiation and residence-time specifications, plus unjustified transfers and possible sulfide-induced catalyst passivation. The Biochemical label alone does not define conditions for the abiotic metal-catalysed steps. Supported branches make leucine production credible, but do not validate every included transformation or the complete environmental implementation. No penalty is applied for the chosen starting inventories, route count, shared intermediates, environment count, low selectivity or racemic output. The network-level confidence is not a simple average of its ten variants. At 0.73, the complete network is not approved against the required 0.90 threshold.

reactions.hint: balanceable if adding: H2 as product; NH3 as product; CO2 as reactant; CO as reactant
